name: Aden Durde

views.text: In the spring, mistakes are how players learn the scheme; speed and communication come first.
A coordinator who does not call plays earns his keep by seeing what the head coach might miss.
Being a first is less important than doing the job well.
Good players can come from anywhere if someone opens the door.
Take the weight off the play-caller on game day: handle personnel and quick fixes on the sideline.
A clear vision from the head coach is what gets a defense to buy in.

signatures: slips British expressions into football talk with his players
plays down his trailblazing status and steers back to the work
want: to earn his own play-calling job and keep widening the path into the NFL for players and coaches from outside America
fear: that working beside a head coach who calls the defense keeps his own contribution unseen
voice: Low-key, warm and direct, with a London accent and an easy manner. He talks about learning, support and the head coach's vision rather than himself, and stays calm and forward-looking. Colleagues describe him as transparent and straight with everyone.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (All Seahawks), Corbin K. Smith
evidence.summary: Macdonald says Durde's record and recommendations put him on the list and their shared view of defending modern offenses won the job; notes Quinn valued Durde in Atlanta and brought him to Dallas. Macdonald's words.

Profile: Middlesex-born linebacker in NFL Europe and on practice squads, London Warriors DC, NFL UK development head, Falcons via a diversity fellowship under Quinn, Cowboys line coach 2021-2023; Jeff Ulbrich calls him a transparent, direct person and close friend. Team site.
With Macdonald calling the defense, Durde says his role will be built over time and he is focused on learning to support the head coach; described as low-key and present-focused. Local report.

Feature: he helped build the International Player Pathway at NFL UK, became the first British full-time NFL coach and first British coordinator, followed Quinn to Dallas, and calls the work more important than being a pioneer; Ulbrich praises his transparency. Feature with quotes.
In OTAs he prioritizes pre-snap speed, communication and alignment over mastery, treats errors as learning, and says players are buying into Macdonald's clear vision. His words.

Before the opener he says his job is to ease Macdonald's load by handling personnel and sideline fixes and watching for what the head coach might miss; praises Macdonald's in-game processing. His words.
